lines: The last engine never stored a single byte itself.
This one does.
Everything from here is about what that choice actually buys you.
Two batches of data land on the same table, one right after the other.
Does the engine open up what's already there and grow it in place?
Or does it just set the new batch down beside the old one?
answer: It sets it down beside the old one.
Each batch becomes its own separate, untouched file.

lines: Two batches, two separate files, neither one ever rewritten in place.
Ask the engine to tidy up, and it reads both, writes a fresh combined file, and retires the old pair.
Count the rows before and after that cleanup: identical.
Here's the payoff for sorting a table by time.
Ask for a single hour out of a much bigger stretch of data.
The engine doesn't scan the stretch. It jumps straight to the one small slice that could possibly match.
Now filter on something the table was never sorted by.
Intuition says that column gets a full scan, no shortcuts available.
Is intuition right here?
answer: A separate structure, built just for that column, skips most of the work anyway.

lines: That separate structure just remembers the low and high value seen in each chunk.
Nothing fancy, and it still throws out most chunks without reading a single row from them.
Sort order was never the only way in.
Set up a second table that only ever holds a running total.
Now write new rows into the first table and walk away -- no further command issued.
The running total updates itself, because writing into the first table is the trigger.
Write the same identifying key twice, with two different payloads.
Ask for it back right away, before any cleanup runs: both versions answer.
Only once a cleanup pass actually runs does one of them quietly disappear.
Ask to remove some rows, and the count drops the moment you ask.
But nothing on disk got smaller yet -- those rows are stamped, not erased.
The real rewrite only happens the next time a cleanup pass touches that data.
Files that never get edited, two separate ways of skipping data nobody needs, a table that updates itself on write, versions that survive until cleanup decides otherwise.
All of that from owning the storage directly.
One more engine still to see: what happens with no server running at all?
